newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FEATURE-Asia struggles for hearts of world-wise youth.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Asia struggles for hearts of world-wise youth.

text.p: Who said the generation gap was a social torment peculiar only to the developed, affluent West?

Across the vast swath of Asia, from the richest countries to the poorest, a familiar pattern is unfolding three decades after a pop culture-driven wave of youth rebellion shook the social foundations of America and Europe.

Whether borne by the technicolor rain of satellite TV or the battering ram of free trade, the visions and values of an outside and largely Western world have penetrated Asia's once-sheltered societies in the 1990s as never before.

Young people, or so an older generation says, are spurning traditional Asian values of collective duty and filial respect to embrace the very vices that have corrupted the West -- sex, drugs and rock 'n' roll.
Filipino teens don the baggy, in-your-face, hip-hop fashions that have bedevilled many American parents for a decade.
Purple-haired punks rattle their elders in largely Moslem Malaysia. Young Bangladeshis and Thais experiment with designer drugs like Ecstasy and more basic over-the-counter opiates.

"Amphetamines have penetrated every walk of life, including school children and Buddhist monks," lamented lawmaker Sophon Phetsawang after Thailand's parliament made the death penalty available for convicted amphetamine traffickers.
In many places, a backlash has already begun.
Youth suicide, homicide, violence and alcoholism are on the rise in parts of Asia, with experts blaming the permissiveness that often comes when both parents work outside the home.

Even in ostensibly regimented socialist states like China and Vietnam, many young people scorn the model workers said to embody their elders' ideals -- preferring the lustier Baywatch models and pop music icons beamed in on satellite television.
In India, sociologists say satellite TV has dramatically altered wealthier teens' values since arriving in 1991.

"Satellite television distorts the way teenagers look at sex. Young people don't feel inhibited any more...," said psychologist Vasantha Patri. "The traditional values that Indians promoted were restrained denial, doing with what you have and aspiring within limits -- which have all but vanished."
Ironically, Japan's soaring affluence has actually fostered abuses like teen prostitution that long were assumed to be the trappings of poverty in less-developed neighbouring countries.
Japanese girls as young as 13 sell their bodies to satisfy the "Lolita complexes" of middle-aged men -- and to earn cash for designer clothes and other expensive luxuries.

Fearing that a generation may be slipping away, many Asian civic groups and governments are fighting back with measures ranging from values education and compulsory national service to tough new laws, late-night curfews and anti-vice dragnets.
Sri Lanka is forming a Child Protection Authority to oversee a national campaign against youth-centred sex tourism -- seen as the most serious problem facing the island's young.

In South Korea, where a cautious opening to global trade has raised living standards but also brought new market challenges, the government is drafting a "Teenager Protection Law" to shelter Korean youths from unwanted foreign influences.

"As Korea opens its markets, all sorts of harmful culture has made its way into the lives of our teenagers -- especially pirated versions of Japanese comic books," said Choi Jin of the culture and sport ministry's Youth Guidance Division.

In Taiwan, where the 1987 lifting of martial law heralded a democratic renaissance, officials are proud of the island's vast new freedoms and wealth but also worry about the late-night licentiousness that so tempts its teens.
The answer? A midnight curfew in the capital Taipei enforced by police equipped with M-16 rifles and bulletproof vests.

"When I go out for fun there are always restrictions," groused 17-year-old Lin Chin-fa, who on a recent late night out beat the curfew by bringing along his father. "I wish they could make it later -- two or three o'clock."

Discipline-minded Singapore is trying controversial measures such as punishment of parents for their childrens' crimes and "reintegrative shaming", in which young offenders and their parents are chastised in public.

Malaysia has gradually intensified its crackdown on youth rebelliousness, restricting nightclubs and video parlours seen as incubators of youthful vice and most recently forbidding anyone under 18 to smoke or possess cigarettes.

"We don't beat up people," a 15-year old Kuala Lumpur skinhead told a local newspaper in response to Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's charge that punk culture was stupid. "It's the music and the looks. It's just for effect," the boy said.
With Malaysia and much of Asia embracing the Internet and other border-blind multimedia technologies, experts say such alien affectations are sure to spread.

"Because of globalisation, young people are beginning to sound, act, and even look more and more alike. Our young people are thinking more like their Western counterparts," said Amina Rasul Bernardo of the Philippines National Youth Commission.

Bernardo cited research showing that, beneath it all, "young Filipinos generally are no different from their parents in that they are God centred, family oriented, desirous of good marriage", though Western influence was becoming a problem.

Malaysia's Mahathir, who like most Asian leaders believes that local values can undergird a globally interconnected society, says that enlightened, religion-based education rather than isolation and discipline is the ultimate guide for youth.
"We have to actually teach them how to lead a good lifestyle and maintain good social behaviour," he said. "It (religious education) should be aimed at shaping good character."
